opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a fascinating story, and in some ways a bit of a surprise to a lot of people in the West. If you'd asked most folks two or three years ago where the frontier of open models would be, they'd probably have said Meta, maybe Mistral in Europe. And then over the course of 2024 and into 2025 you saw Qwen from Alibaba, DeepSeek, and then a whole wave after that: Moonshot with Kimi, Zhipu, MiniMax. Suddenly a lot of the strongest open-weight models on the Hugging Face Hub were coming from Chinese labs.

How I understand it, there are a few things going on. One is very pragmatic. If you're a Chinese lab and you're a bit behind on compute because of export controls, and you're also a bit behind on the brand recognition that OpenAI or Anthropic have globally, open-sourcing is a fantastic way to get adoption. You put out a great model, developers everywhere pick it up, fine-tune it, build on it, and you become part of the default toolkit. It's a distribution strategy as much as anything. That's how you win mindshare when you can't necessarily win on a closed API in Western markets.

The second thing is that constraints actually breed creativity. DeepSeek is the classic example. They had to be extremely efficient: mixture-of-experts done really well, clever attention tricks, low-precision training, very careful engineering of the whole stack. And then they published it. They wrote really detailed papers, shared the recipes. That's something we used to see a lot more from American labs and have seen less of recently. So there's a culture of open research there that, honestly, reminds me of the earlier days of deep learning.

Third, I think there's an ecosystem effect inside China itself. Once a couple of labs went open and got a lot of credit for it, there was competitive pressure for others to follow. Open became the norm, and it's hard to be the one lab that keeps everything closed when your peers are getting all the attention for releasing.

From where we sit at Hugging Face, it's a bit of a wake-up call. I've been saying for a while that the US and Europe shouldn't cede open source. Open models are how you build a broad research community, how startups get started, how universities stay relevant, how you get transparency and trust. If the best open models in the world are mostly coming from one country, that shapes the whole ecosystem: what people build on, what values or defaults get baked in. So I see China's emergence as both genuinely impressive and a signal that the West needs to reinvest in open science, whether that's through companies, through public funding, or through efforts like ours to build fully open models with the data and training code released too.

r001.rationale: The response says that after some labs released models, competitive pressure led others to follow, making openness a norm among Chinese labs.

r002.rationale: Zhipu is named among Chinese labs, but the response does not say it stopped open-sourcing or that doing so reduced its appeal to prospective employees.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a fascinating story, and I think it surprised a lot of people, but honestly it shouldn't have.

If you look at the history, China's AI community was always quite deeply embedded in the open ecosystem. Alibaba, Baidu, the academic labs, they were publishing papers, releasing code, contributing to PyTorch, all of that for years. So the culture was there. What changed is the strategic calculus.

When you're the challenger, open source is your best weapon. If you're behind the frontier labs in the US, and you can't match their distribution or their brand or their compute, then giving your model away is how you get adoption. Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, these teams understood that releasing open weights means thousands of developers around the world building on your stack, fine-tuning it, benchmarking it, and essentially becoming your evangelists for free. You win mindshare, and mindshare translates into talent, into ecosystem, and eventually into revenue through the cloud.

There's also a very practical point about chip restrictions. When you're constrained on compute, you're forced to be efficient, and efficiency innovations are exactly the kind of thing that open releases showcase. DeepSeek is the perfect example. They couldn't just throw more GPUs at the problem, so they innovated on architecture and training recipes, and then they published everything. That was a huge credibility moment.

And then I think there's a geopolitical layer. Open-source models from China become a form of soft power. If the dominant open models that developers in Europe, in Africa, in Southeast Asia are building on come from China, that's influence. Meanwhile, the American labs went in the opposite direction. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, they mostly closed up, and Meta was the big exception for a while, but even they wavered. So there was a vacuum, and China filled it.

At Hugging Face we see this very directly. For a long time the most downloaded models were from Meta or from Mistral, and now a large share of the top trending models are Chinese. Developers don't really care where a model comes from. They care whether it's good, whether the license is permissive, and whether it runs on their hardware.

The thing I'd push back on a bit is the framing of China as a "champion" in some ideological sense. I don't think it's ideological at all. It's pragmatic. And the moment the incentives shift, if one of these labs gets to the frontier and feels it has a lead worth protecting, you may see them close up too. So I think the lesson for the rest of us, and especially for Europe, is not to rely on anyone's generosity. Open source is strongest when there are many players contributing for their own reasons, and that's what we should be building toward.

r001.rationale: The response describes openness as a strategy for gaining adoption and mindshare, but does not say Chinese AI providers compete with one another on openness.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Zhipu or connect a decision to stop open-sourcing models with reduced appeal to prospective employees.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things to separate: the motivation to release models openly, and the impact those releases have. The motivation can be strategic—you want developers to use your models, build on them, and make your technology part of the ecosystem. But the impact can still be very positive for openness.

And I’d be careful about treating China as a single actor here. There are different companies and research teams making different choices. The interesting question is what they actually release. Can you download the weights? Can you modify the model and use it commercially? Do you have enough information about the training to reproduce it? Those are different levels of openness.

For me, the opportunity is that more people can participate. If strong models are available openly, a small team anywhere can study them and build something useful. But that openness needs to be durable. You don’t want the whole ecosystem to depend on one company, or one country, continuing to release its next model.

r001.rationale: The response notes that Chinese companies and research teams make different release choices, but does not say they compete with one another on openness.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Zhipu, stopping open releases, or prospective employees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very significant shift. For a long time, people assumed that the strongest AI models would come from a handful of American companies, and that those companies would become increasingly closed. What we’re seeing from China challenges both assumptions.

There’s a strong practical reason to release models openly: it helps you build an ecosystem. Developers around the world can use your models, adapt them, and build tools around them. That’s a powerful way to compete, especially when you’re challenging an established leader.

I would distinguish open weights from fully open source, though. Being able to download a model is valuable, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you have the training data or the code needed to reproduce it.

For me, the encouraging part is that this makes AI less dependent on a few companies. The question is whether that openness lasts as these companies become more successful. I’d judge that by what they continue to share, rather than assuming openness belongs to any particular country.

r001.rationale: The response describes openness as a way China can compete with established leaders, but does not say Chinese AI providers compete with one another on openness.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Zhipu, stopping open-sourcing models, or effects on prospective employees.
